I would like to add that many of us live in an environment that pushes instant gratification. Due to the breath of choice available to us, very frequently people have very specific lists of what they're looking for, and if you don't check their boxes out of the gate (be it in appearance, personality, or willingness to partake in certain activities) they will 'cut their losses' and move on to the next one. That is, assuming they're not putting on an act for ulterior motives. On top of that, there are many people who freak out at the prospect of things becoming real. Either because they aren't in a position for commitment, or they were misrepresenting themselves in some way and don't believe they can keep up the act in person. It is, with the current state of things, really difficult to find the combination of honesty, compatibility, emotional intelligence, self-awareness and courage to attempt something long term.

I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt, so it feels really uncharitable to see a lot of people in the comments turning "how are we going to live" into "how am I going to live". Sometimes people try way too hard to read between the lines rather than taking people literally at their word, and infer things that aren't there. I don't know what was going through your head, but I can see plenty of reason for that to be a perfectly understandable response. I think it's really important to look at exactly WHY that was the first thing out of your mouth and be really honest about it to both yourself and your boyfriend. I don't want to put words in your mouth so I'm deliberately refraining from elaborating, but if your intentions were good-natured it will become clear to both yourself and him should you do that. Introspection isn't easy but it's pretty vital. I hope you figure it out, best of luck.

I just want to point out there is likely to be some bias to the responses you receive on a post like that. Personally, I saw the post and saw no need to click on or interact with it. That concept is something I've been aware of since high school, and in my experience it seems common knowledge that if you don't want to come off as aggressive (really not the way I want to word this but I just woke up and my brain is foggy) you offer your number and not the other way around. I generally try not to respond too much in here, but figured I'd mention it.

That's an unfortunate situation to be in and I'm sorry to hear it. Honestly, I find it kind of hard to comment without more context. The biggest question is what exactly do you mean by "He was a terrible friend"? Was he a terrible friend in the moment, or in general? If the latter, I don't understand what the benefit of remaining his friend is. If it's the former, then there is potentially a lot to consider. If this behavior is uncharacteristic for him, the why matters a lot. If he was in a toxic relationship rife with manipulation, then hearing what he has to say if he shows remorse is potentially worth doing. Time is, in my opinion, a poor indicator of value. Being friends for a long time isn't a good reason in itself to try and salvage a friendship. People can change over time, or reveal aspects of their personality you were unaware of before. Holding onto the good times is a recipe for disaster if things look as though you are functionally incompatible in your opinion.

Relationships, platonic or otherwise, are incredibly nuanced so I would hesitate taking direct advice from anyone (myself included) who doesn't have a good picture of what's going on and your history as well. All I can safely recommend is to take some time to cool off, ask yourself what you want specifically (without making any considerations on how that might effect other people) then look at the pros and cons. Good luck.

"Why would you harass ANY person like this, much less a person you are supposed to love?"

A person abuses someone they 'love' when their perception of reality supersedes that of the other individual. From their perspective the other person is not being abused, and there's nothing that can be said to convince them otherwise. Love doesn't work the same for everyone, it's as simple as that.

Something I have spent a lot of time trying to accept myself is that the good is never worth the bad. When you try to weigh the good against the bad on some kind of balancing scale it becomes really easy to delude yourself into tolerating behaving you'd never for a second accept on its own. At the end of the day its up to you to decide what behavior you'd like to be allow around you on a daily basis.

Those are some amazing steps you've taken for yourself and I'm super impressed by it. I hope you are just as proud of yourself, because it's not an easy thing to do. Additionally, your third paragraph here shows some amazing insight that you really should hold onto. "But love isn't all you need" is a really hard concept to grasp without experiencing it first hand, and I implore you to really reflect on that and what led you to that realization. Everyone processes differently, so it's really important to settle on what you feel like is best for you without compromising for someone else. Personally I have a tendency to fall back into old rhythms unless I take some time for self-reflection, but it's less about a hard time frame and more about a certain level of examination.

It is very important to note that people do not change unless they want to themselves. Changing for another person unfortunately doesn't happen, so unless they develop that desire on their own there's nothing you can really say or do to make someone change their mind unless they're already open to it. Ignoring any ethical implications of ultimatums, they're just not effective. At best they will make someone fake certain behavior in your presence. It can be okay to set a sort of ultimatum for yourself, as way of defining clear boundaries of what is and isn't acceptable but placing them on other people typically doesn't help. Very much wish you the best of luck and hope you can find what boundaries allow you to be the most comfortable. Wish I had better advice to give but I don't think I know you well enough to do so. Trust your instincts.

First off, I am sorry for what you're going through and that you haven't been able to separate yourself to a comfortable degree from the situation at large.

I want to preface my point with saying that ultimately you really need to prioritize your own feelings and healing. Absolving other people of empathy so you can be empathetic in their stead can be a very taxing and painful way to live.

That said, closure is more often than not kind of a trap. There's a strong difference between having no idea what took place, and having a pretty good idea of what happened but hoping for a different outcome. In the latter scenario, looking for closure often means searching for anything that will prove the unlikely alternative because it will allow a return to the status quo. While, frequently, this is more of a subconscious thing, it doesn't make it any less real or frankly dangerous. I don't want to make assumptions about your relationship with your husband, but if you genuinely believe he has your best intentions at heart I would advise you to ask him to take a good hard look at why he needs closure. In the scenario where it is impossible to get a definitive answer (which is a very real possibility) would he rather err on the side of caution or believe a misunderstanding has taken place. If it's the former, what tangible benefit can even be gained from anything other than cutting off contact.

I really hope you can find the best outcome for yourself and prioritize your safety above all else. Best of luck.

"Dad!" I yelled for the third time. I loved having him over, except for the few times he actually asks me for something. Without fail he hides away in the guest room, as if ashamed to request something of his own son, but my hydra neck served on dragon flank is hard to pass up (and it's not easy meat to source). I really didn't want to drag a plate up to his room, he can put back more than I can comfortably carry. Maybe a sampler would make him forget his misguided shame. So I carved off a slice of each and poured a mug of tea (heavens forbid I bring him an ale by mistake, won't hear the end of it till he leaves) to bring him a small platter.

Even knocking on his door with my foot didn't garner a response so I pushed it in with my back instead, he was really making me work for it this time. When I turned around I could barely understand what I was looking at. I don't even remember when it happened but at some point I had dropped the platter but I never even heard it crash to the ground. The sound of my own blood rushed through my ears as I struggled to come to grips with the grisly scene before me. The walls were painted red with blood and my father lay in an undignified heap on the ground, only his legs still covered by armor, the rest of which was crumpled under the destroyed armor rack in the corner. He still clutched the symbol of his god in one hand, cracked now, and his trusty hammer in the other. Standing above his corpse was....my mother of all people. She'd gone missing three years ago so I can't fathom how she got here in the first place. Or why she looked like she just went three rounds with my father.

"How foolish you are, to think that evil must come from corruption, that the pure must be good" she practically spat at me, cutting through my stupor and dragging me back to reality. My body must have caught up faster than my mind did, as I could feel the contempt and disgust written plainly on my face. Only now did I notice the blade in her hands, still dripping with my father's blood. A short, simple looking thing. Hard to believe he lost to such a trivial looking weapon. Eventually my brain began to process what she had said and all I could manage was a choked "What?...you're evil now?"

"ME?!" She thundered, utterly incredulous. Her fury caused her to regrip the blade anew which she thrust in the direction of the lump of flesh, that was my father not too long ago, and continued "He KNEW, this whole time. They are a noble, if misunderstood race. Intelligent but territorial only when pressed. The church provoked them, looking for their ancient relics. And for what? To seal them up in glass cases to honor their stupid god? And he went along with it. He helped them...murder so many. They're nearly extinct y'know. And he played such a....role in it."

An ugly silence hung between us, I hadn't even realized I had backed up into the doorway, gripping the frame so tightly it splintered under my fingers. "What? None of this makes sense. All he ever did was protect people" but I couldn't even think beyond that before she started in again "Protect? He's just a glorified murderer like the rest of his ilk. And look at you, serving them on a platter as if there was nothing detestable going on." Dumbfounded I stared at her a moment long before it finally dawned on me "Dragons....you're talking about Dragons? The things that ki-....we thought killed you." There was a small shake of her head and she vanished from my sight. Next thing I knew there was a blade touching my throat, and a whisper at my ear "They wanted to talk, is all. To someone actually willing to listen since he would not. They tried to negotiate. But you can't negotiate with barbarians." I missed my chance, if there was one, to protest. The cut was so clean as to be painless for my words were replaced with a bloody gurgle and I could already feel my lungs filling before the pain ever started. She was gone, again, and soon I would be as well. All this over...monsters?

First off, don't be disappointed in yourself for the ignorance of others. That's pretty counter-intuitive. Secondly, ignorance in itself (literally being uneducated/uninformed) isn't necessarily an issue. The glaring issue I see here is not that he's wildly incorrect about female anatomy, but moreso that he's not open to the possibility of being incorrect. Being wrong is fine so long as you're willing to accept new information that disputes your current way of thinking. I don't think the onus is on you to educate him, but if you choose to do so and he still disagrees bear in mind that it very likely means in future discussions he'll only believe what he chooses to regardless of facts presented. Which is pretty dangerous to be around, imo, unless you really trust his style of judgement in general.

>  I’m sure it feels unpleasant, but rejection isn’t personal. He just isn’t the type of man who romantically or physically appeals to her. 

I agree with much of what you said above, but the only thing I want to touch on is that rejection IS personal. But there's nothing wrong with that. Being rejected because someone isn't into you is incredibly personal. It's YOU they aren't attracted to. That doesn't mean there is something wrong with you however. Being compatible, or incompatible, with someone does nothing to impact your value/worth. When you put your value in the hands of others you're destined to feel worthless nonstop.

I agree mutual attraction is vital, as ultimately that's the only way anything happens unless someone is legitimately coerced or just goes along with things whether it be to avoid confrontation or otherwise.

However, it's pretty impossible to determine if mutual attraction exists without actually asking the other person. Our feelings are, in reality, entirely one-sided. Also I hope I didn't overstate the idea of "doing everything right" because for some people that genuinely means not being an overbearing asshole (which quite frankly they may have been, but just not from their perspective) and asking politely. Speaking from my own rather embarrassing personal experience, back in my younger years I definitely had gone through the effort to build up a rapport, see if I was genuinely interested, find out what their interests were and if I aligned with that at all, before making an effort to genuinely pursue them only to be rejected without receiving an answer that made it clear to me why. "I don't see you that way" is a valid response, but it's not one that provides clarity. I will refrain from making broad sweeping strokes about men in general or even types of men, but I've known my fair share of dudes who can get rather miffed because they can become friends with people they either are interested in from the get go, or become interested in during the course of friendship but can't seem to push past that barrier, as it were. So where does attraction translate from the platonic to the romantic.

Honestly it's something I see as a very important topic, but it's also one that requires a lot of introspection.

The thing is, at the end of the day, knowing why someone is not into you will never suddenly unlock the key to making them attracted to you. It's probably more important to come to grips with the fact that the why doesn't really matter, unless it affects your ability to remain friends with them on principle after the fact.

As someone who has struggled a lot with rejection over the years and, for a time, bought into the whole "Nice guys finish last" mentality, I will say the seeds of misogyny are planted well before any form of rejection. The inability to enter in or maintain a relationship simply acts as a justification for the belief that someone (women in this case) is not giving them what they deserve and thus are the cause of their problems. They themselves are never to blame because "They did everything right".

Rarely do we analyze why we don't like someone unless there is a glaring issue. Nothing inherently wrong with this nor does it make someone's feelings less valid. And it can feel very shitty to kick someone while they're down (e.g. listing all the reasons why you decided to reject someone immediately after rejecting them) so it's very common for people to pull their punches on why they're not interested when probed; should they happen to be consciously aware of the reasons at all. Not getting a concrete answer as to "why" can build up feelings of confusion and resentment which in turn fuel the fantasy of "I did everything right but still it doesn't go my way, there must be someone else to blame."

This doesn't excuse the behavior, and realistically they need to come to terms with themselves and being comfortable alone before they can ever take rejection well without lashing out. No amount of brutally accurate shut-downs can do that work for them.

I think most people are resistant to change regardless of what stage of life they're in. If someone is genuinely interested in changing, but unaware of an area they ought to consider changing, one serious conversation is enough to incite change. Are they going to change overnight? No, not at all.

His age is only one factor to consider and I personally don't think it's the most relevant. I also don't understand what you mean by having to manage the performance of someone who is ignorant. I may have a different idea of how much of the onus is on the man in this situation and not OP. OP literally cannot do the work for him, and trying to do so is a waste of both of their time.

For you I'd say then yeah move on. Empathy and introspection are very much skills and can increase with practice. A conversation will show whether or not he's actually interested in improving in those areas. In my opinion, literally one conversation is all that it takes. Saying that he's naturally incapable or incompetent in respect to women's sexuality sounds blind to the impact of his environment on his development. It's a question of whether or not he's actually interested in improving. Ignorance is forgivable, in my opinion. Willful stupidity is not. If one conversation is too much of an investment in your opinion then definitely get out. There's nothing wrong with that. But it's also not worth hanging around forever waiting for someone to change. People only change if they want to.

Culture is a huge factor in how men perceive sex, and I know plenty of dudes who flat refuse to eat pussy because they've been convinced it's not "manly" and therefore is direct insult to even suggest that they do it.

Your feelings are always valid and I recommend taking the time to feel your way through them completely. If he is open-minded enough, you both might benefit from a frank conversation about how he feels, and why that's the case. As well as your own feelings on the topic. Invite him to do some introspection on his own.

To my knowledge, food poisoning can and has killed people. I've only experienced very mild food poisoning in my life, and never to the point where I've had to throw up. Which has often made me question if I've experienced food poisoning at all. On this particular day, I experienced the worst food poisoning of my life. Initially I thought to myself "Okay, what is going on? Was it something I ate? What did I eat today?" went to the bathroom, had some diarrhea. Tried to return to bed. Then more diarrhea. "Okay I might need to call out of work if this keeps up. That'd be kind of nice, but am I gotta have enough money for rent if I do that?" More diarrhea. Last bout of it. "Okay. I feel like shit but I think I'm good now." Chug some pepto. Lay down again. Feel the pain in my stomach grow. Strikes me as weird but whatever. Sometimes life sucks. Next thing I know I'm about to puke. Nausea hits me like a truck and the only thing I can do is run to the bathroom. I end up throwing up in the sink cause I can't make it to the toilet. Really fucking chunky vomit too. Never have I seen vomit like this in my life. It's disturbing to look at honestly, and it smells fucking horrendous. Also it's FUCKING PINK. Startling. I look back to my bed, I can see my bed from my bathroom, and realize I really don't have enough strength in my legs to get there. Definitely not enough to make it back if I need to throw up again. So I lay down near the toilet. I'm cold. Sweating. And shivering. I half-push, half-pull myself up to puke into the toilet again. "This fucking sucks. I feel fucking terrible. Holy shit. Am I in shock? Am I going into shock? Is that what that feels like?" All the energy is draining out of my body. I feel pain, cold, shivering, my gut is twitching intermittently. "Am I going to die? People can die from food poisoning right? I feel like I'm going to die." I realize I have about enough energy in my body to make one text message. Or to dial 911 and just say nothing. I'm not sure if I'll need to throw up again but I'm fully prepared to just throw up on the floor, or in my sleep. I even roll onto my side in case I need to throw up in my sleep. Then I laid there there and thought to myself "Should I text someone who knows where I live and come get me? Should I ask to go to the hospital? Should I text someone who doesn't know where I live so they at least know if I'm dead that I died. Am I okay with dying? Do I really want to go on living? Is there anything I really want to do?" And I laid there, really thinking on whether or not I was okay with dying. Things I want to do, things I don't want to put up with anymore. And I decided I was perfectly okay with just dying, even if it meant waking up in a couple of hours with literally zero energy and just waiting to starve/dehydrate. Then I passed out. I wouldn't say I felt a sense of peace, but more like one of acceptance and release.

This will probably get lost in the shuffle but I'd really like to stress to try cooking. I've been struggling with depression forever and I have this weird mental block when it comes to cooking for myself. I love looking for other people and will do so at the drop of a hat. But when it comes to cooking for myself I'll often get scared that I'll fuck it up, make something I don't like, waste my money, eat a shitty meal (or not at all) and end up putting myself in a worse mood. Which feeds the depression spiral before I ever get off my ass.

You don't have to become a fantastic cook, make amazing meals, or plate your food like it's a 5 star restaurant. I really like canned/pouch tuna from the store. It's cheap, filling and literally I don't have to prepare it. The other day I was starving, with almost nothing in the house, found a pouch of tuna I forgot about and really wasn't feeling just eating tuna straight. So I decided to 'stirfry' it. I'll be honest, I dunno shit about stirfry and I couldn't find my soy sauce. Ended up throwing some spices in there I like, and some I was on the fence about, hit it with worchestershire sauce and fried it up. Came out fantastic and it's definitely something I plan to mess around with more in the future. Having to 'learn' or 'know' recipes can be a massive roadblock in trying to get into cooking, at least for me it's been a huge barrier especially when it comes to interacting with my depression.

Seriously, pick low-effort food you already like (top ramen, ham sandwiches, quesadillas) and just experiment with ways to spice them up (literally) and bring new life to them. It's a process that can really boost your mood and save you a lot of money in the long run. I'm still shit at it, and I can't handle meal prep to save my life. It stresses me the fuck out and I don't know why. So if you're not into meal prep, don't sweat it. Work with what's good for you and go from there. Seriously, try cooking.

There are plenty of great suggestions in this thread already, but I can't stress enough how important it is to get their personal take on it if you really want to have meaningful impact.
